html:
The Byzantine Empire was the eastern half of the Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, which carried on after the west fell and lasted until 1453. It has no founding date of its own: the chart starts it at the final split of 395. Its people called themselves Romans; "Byzantine" is a label invented by later Western scholars.

It was Greek speaking, Orthodox Christian and governed by an emperor and a trained bureaucracy, with Roman law at its core. Its capital, founded by Constantine, was the largest and richest city in Christendom for centuries, guarded by great land walls and the sea.

Key moments:

  • Justinian (527 to 565) codified Roman law, built Hagia Sophia and won back Italy and Africa, but the plague cut his gains short.
  • In the 600s Heraclius beat Persia, then lost Syria and Egypt to the Arab conquests.
  • Iconoclasm split the Church over images in the 700s and 800s.
  • Basil II brought a high point around 1000, and the Rus' took Christianity from Constantinople.
  • Defeat by the Seljuk Turks at Manzikert in 1071 cost most of Anatolia.

The worst blow came from fellow Christians, when the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204. The empire was restored in 1261 but was now a small state squeezed by Venice, Serbia and the Ottomans. Mehmed II took the city in the Fall of Constantinople in 1453. Its scholars and manuscripts helped feed the Italian Renaissance.
